title: Do we know whether our risk-scoring algorithms are equally accurate across demographic groups?
description: A board-level oversight question testing whether an organisation has actually measured — not assumed — that a risk-scoring algorithm's errors are evenly distributed across protected groups, and whether any proxy variable it relies on has been scrutinised.
question_text: For every risk-scoring algorithm we use in a high-stakes decision, can management show us the false-positive and false-negative rates broken out by protected group — not just an aggregate accuracy number — and can they name every proxy variable the model relies on and justify why it isn't a stand-in for a protected characteristic?
rationale: Both COMPAS and a major US healthcare risk-prediction algorithm looked reasonable on aggregate accuracy while hiding large, harmful disparities that only appeared once results were disaggregated by group — in the healthcare case, traced to an unexamined proxy variable (cost) standing in for actual need.
follow_up_actions: Request the most recent fairness metrics report for every in-scope risk-scoring model.
Ask what proxy variables the model uses and whether their correlation with protected characteristics has been tested.
Confirm the analysis is re-run whenever the model or its training data changes materially.

citations.title: Machine Bias — There's Software Used Across the Country to Predict Future Criminals. And It's Biased Against Blacks.
